b: I love that many of the submissions we receive are pieces I could never have imagined writing. Samy’s piece is something I could never have written, since it is inspired by something I would never have read. Now, however, Knock ou le Triomphe de la médecine has risen to the top of my Goodreads list.

Preparing for my end-of-year exams, caught between hospital shifts and studying, I had no mental energy left for books and stopped reading entirely for months. When summer arrived, I wanted to get back into the habit with an ambitious reading list. But before tackling any doorstopper, I needed an easy win to build momentum.

Looking for a short classic with enough literary weight to shamelessly harvest some cultural capital with minimal effort, I picked up Jules Romains’ 1923 satirical play: Knock ou le Triomphe de la médecine (Doctor Knock, or the Triumph of Medicine).

I expected a museum piece about old-fashioned country quacks. Instead, I was floored by a work that revealed that a century ago, a French audience laughed at the problems we still debate: lowering diagnostic thresholds, the financial lure of chronic treatment, and the obsession with self-monitoring.

In France, Knock is an enduring classic, largely thanks to Louis Jouvet’s legendary stage and screen performances. The translations quoted below are my own, aimed at restoring Romains’ sharp comedic satire.
The Setup: Creating a Market Out of Nothing

The play opens in a rattling car crawling up a mountain road. Dr. Parpalaid is selling his rural practice to newcomer Dr. Knock. For thirty years, he coasted: reassuring patients, prescribing herbal tea, and collecting modest fees. He believes a physician can only wait for disease to arrive. Knock knows better: you manufacture it.

Three months later, Parpalaid returns to find the town transformed: the hotel is an overflowing clinic, the pharmacist is prospering, and the once-healthy villagers are bedridden on long, costly regimens. Watching Knock build his empire feels less like vintage farce and more like a blueprint of modern medical economics, with mechanisms we still wrestle with today.
No Healthy People, Only Undiagnosed Ones

A recurring lesson on Sensible Medicine is how lowering diagnostic thresholds turns healthy people into patients. Knock builds his entire practice on this premise. Early in the play, Knock tells Parpalaid that his doctoral thesis opened with a line he wrongly attributed to Claude Bernard:
“Healthy people are merely sick people unaware of their condition.”
Later, while recruiting the village pharmacist, Mousquet, Knock dismisses the very concept of being well, claiming modern science has rendered “health” obsolete:

‘Falling sick’ is an obsolete notion that no longer stands up before the data of modern science. Health is merely a word that could be struck from our vocabulary without the slightest inconvenience. For my part, I recognize only people more or less afflicted with more or less numerous diseases progressing at a more or less rapid pace.

Curing an acute problem pays once; managing a chronic condition can pay indefinitely. Knock grasps this immediately. Late in the play, he shows Parpalaid his charts: one-off consultations have stalled, but long-term home treatments have exploded:
“In itself, the consultation only half-interests me; it is a rather crude art, a kind of net fishing. But treatment, that is fish farming.”
Captive customers for years. Every villager sent to bed is tracked with a pin on a district map, his conquest charted house by house.

The play's funniest scene shows a healthy man turned into a distressed patient. Knock hires the village crier to advertise free Monday consultations. When the crier asks for a free one himself, Knock asks what ails him. The man searches for some stray sensation:
THE CRIER: “Wait, let me think! … Well, after dinner, there are times I feel a sort of sensation here. It tickles me, or rather, it prickles me.”
Knock adopts an air of grave authority:
KNOCK: “Careful. Let us not confuse terms. Does it tickle you, or does it prickle you?”
THE CRIER: “It prickles… But it tickles a bit, too.”

Knock pushes a finger hard into the man’s abdomen: “Does it hurt when I push my finger in?” The crier, startled that getting forcefully jabbed in the stomach hurts, answers with genuine surprise: “Yes… it actually does hurt!”
Then Knock asks: “Doesn’t it prickle more when you’ve eaten calf’s head in vinaigrette?” The crier reflects: “I never eat it… but it seems to me that if I did eat it, indeed, it would prickle more.”

Knock turns mundane digestion into a condition caught “just in time.” He forbids wine, tobacco, and marital relations, yet insists the crier finish his rounds first. Terrified, the man leaves in a cold sweat, wondering if he shouldn’t run straight home.
In medicine, we frequently fall into what Nassim Taleb calls Platonicity: mistaking our intellectual models for reality.

Knock pulls this on a wealthy farmer’s wife who consults him because she is tired. Knock asks if she ever fell off a ladder as a child. She doesn’t recall, but Knock insists: a tall ladder, three and a half meters high, landing on her left hip. Swayed by his confidence, she agrees.

Knock reaches for the blackboard and sketches her spinal cord, explaining that her “Türck tract” and “Clarke column” have side-slipped a fraction of a millimeter, straining her multipolar cells. He demands an astronomical fee, and when she hesitates, he sets a self-fulfilling trap: a week in a dark room, curtains drawn, in total silence, with no solid food and only Vichy water. If she feels weak and dizzy by the end, as anyone starved in the dark would, that weakness will prove she needs the full treatment.

From the hotel window in Act III, Knock and Parpalaid look over the dark valley. At ten at night, a farming village should be asleep. Instead, lamps glow across the hills, tracing the borders of Knock’s empire:

“Consider that in a few moments the clock will strike ten; that for all my patients, ten o’clock means the second rectal temperature reading, and that in a few moments, two hundred and fifty thermometers will penetrate simultaneously…”
It is played for laughs, yet it anticipates our modern obsession with harvesting biometric noise, mistaking relentless measurement for health.

Knock’s diagnostic weapon turns on everyone, even himself: “Lately, I’ve had to stop looking at myself in the mirror.” When Parpalaid mocks the scam and tries to leave, Knock tells him he looks ill and unfit to travel. Parpalaid scoffs and refuses at first, but the seed is planted. By the final scene, the skeptic checks into the clinic and climbs into bed as Knock’s latest patient.

What makes Knock extraordinary is that this critique came not in a medical journal but in a mainstream comedy for ordinary playgoers in Paris. The public was laughing at diagnostic creep, biological plausibility, and the commercialization of disease a century before our current debates. Romains’ premise was simple: if health is just an uninvestigated disease, the entire world is a waiting room.
Amieur Samy Abdelmoumene is a medical student at the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Health Sciences in Algiers, Algeria.
